Callisto. The outermost of Jupiter's four large Galilean moons and the third-largest moon in the solar system. Ancient and heavily cratered, Callisto is one of the most crater-scarred bodies in the solar system, suggesting a relatively inert geological history with little tidal heating. Unlike its inner Galilean siblings, Callisto preserves a record of ancient impacts and may harbor a subsurface ocean beneath its icy crust.

Callisto has a diameter of four thousand eight hundred twenty-one kilometers, making it the third-largest moon in the solar system. The surface is heavily cratered and geologically ancient, showing ancient multi-ring impact structures like Gilgamesh with rings extending hundreds of kilometers. Because Callisto is far enough from Jupiter that gravitational stress is minimal, it experiences no apparent tidal heating, unlike Io and Europa.

Callisto was one of the four Galilean moons discovered by Galileo in sixteen ten. Through magnetometry, scientists have detected evidence of a possible subsurface ocean, and the moon's composition is roughly equal parts ice and rock. The dark surface suggests a composition of dark ice mixed with rock dust. Callisto is named after a figure from Greek mythology, a priestess of Hera. Among all the Galilean moons, Callisto offers a stark contrast—while Europa and Ganymede harbor subsurface oceans and exhibit active geology, Callisto's heavily cratered surface tells the story of ancient bombardment and relative stability.
